newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe central bank urges caution over wages.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe central bank urges caution over wages.

text.p: Zimbabwe's central bank, which is battling high inflation, urged wage negotiators on Thursday to ensure that this year's pay rises match the reduced growth rate of productivity.
Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe governor Leonard Tsumba said the bank expected labour productivity to grow at only two percent this year compared with just over six percent last year.

"It is therefore essential that wage negotiations take this fact into account to avoid another inflation spiral. Thus it is of utmost importance that wage and salary awards are commensurate with the reduced productivity level," he said.

"To the extent that final wage settlements are higher than the level consistent with the growth in productivity, inflation will surely rise once again," he said in his first monetary policy statement for 1997.
Zimbabwe wage negotiations normally start in April. Unions have previously vowed to press for pay rises above the rate of annual inflation.
Last year, wage increases averaged about 25 percent compared with average annual inflation of 21.7 percent for the year.

Tsumba reaffirmed forecasts that annual inflation -- which rose to 19 percent in February from 15.8 percent in January -- would be around 19-21 percent by June, above the 17 percent target set in the 1996/97 budget.
He said the rate should be below 20 percent for the remainder of the year but cautioned that these estimates depended on the 1997/98 budget outturn and how it would be financed.
The government presents an 18-month budget in July ahead of adopting the calendar year as the financial year.
Tsumba said the central bank would aim to restrict broad money supply growth to no more than 25 percent from 30 percent in 1996.

"The high level of money expansion in 1996, the commensurate high nominal GDP (gross domestic product) growth notwithstanding, cannot be allowed to continue into 1997, however, as such excessive money growth will not be compatible with the anticipated level of economic activity this year," he said.
Zimbabwe's agricultural-powered economy is expected to grow by about five percent this year -- largely due to a generally favourable 1996/97 farming season -- compared to eight percent last year.

"For this growth to be sustained, however, sound monetary policy will remain crucial. Overall, macroeconomic stability will only come about when both fiscal policy and a supportive productive sector are in line with the bank's monetary policy stance," Tsumba said.
